narrative:
Based on your application, the model estimates that you have a 31% chance of becoming a bad credit risk. That means, for every 100 people with profiles similar to yours, around 31 would likely struggle to repay the loan. While this isn't a majority, it is still high enough that the bank considers the risk unacceptable, which is why your application was denied.

The most important factor in this decision was your checking account status. Your account had a negative balance, a situation seen in only about 12.6% of approved applicants. This strongly signals financial strain and was the single biggest push toward a bad credit risk rating. In fact, this factor alone outweighed the more positive aspects of your profile.

Interestingly, two other notable factors actually worked in your favor. Your installment rate is only 2% of your disposable income, well below the average of about 3% for approved borrowers, showing you have room in your budget. Also, you requested a credit duration of just 12 months, which is much shorter than the typical 19 months, meaning the bank would be exposed for less time. Both of these pushed the model toward considering you a good credit risk.

However, the negative balance in your checking account was so influential that it tipped the overall decision against you. To improve your chances next time, focus on building a positive checking account history by ensuring your balance stays above zero for several months. Additionally, consider reducing your existing debts or increasing your income to lower your debt-to-income ratio further. With consistent financial stability, you can demonstrate to the bank that the risk has decreased.
